checks.claim: Key: with mass fixed, acceleration is directly proportional to net force, so acceleration against pull is a straight line through zero
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'directly proportional to the net force ... inversely proportional to its mass'; OpenStax states the same. Proportional means a straight line through the origin.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'a flat line along zero' (steady pull gives steady speed, the Aristotelian idea)
Wrong: 'rises, then levels off' and 'ever steeper curve' (no friction or other effect named; F = ma is linear in F)
Context: one newton is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s per second
checks.note: Grokipedia: '1 N is defined as the force required to accelerate a 1 kg mass by 1 m/s2'.

checks.claim: Key: same net force on twice the mass gives half the acceleration
checks.note: a = F/m, inversely proportional to mass.

checks.claim: Wrong: just as great / twice / a quarter
Context: loaded truck takes twice as long to reach the same speed (constant acceleration, half the rate)
Key: three equal riders, same acceleration, needs three times the net force
checks.note: F = ma. Strictly the sledge's own mass makes it a little under three times, but the stem calls the sledge light, and any ice friction also grows in step with the load, so 'three times' is the right plain-words answer and no other choice is close.

checks.claim: Wrong: twice / nine times / just as hard
Context: pulling twice as hard on three times the mass gives two-thirds of the acceleration; ice removes friction, not mass
Key: with a steady thrust and falling mass, acceleration grows, greatest just before the fuel runs out
checks.note: Also follows directly from a = F/m (Grokipedia, Newton's laws).

checks.claim: Wrong: stays the same / shrinks / drops to zero once fast
Context: Saturn V first stage's acceleration rose as fuel burned until the crew felt about 4 g; the centre engine was shut down early to limit it
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'To limit acceleration to about 4 g for crew safety as fuel mass decreased, the center F-1 engine underwent cutoff (CECO) at T+2 minutes 15 seconds', before outboard cutoff at T+2:42. Wikipedia (Saturn V): 'As the Saturn V consumed fuel, its weight decreased, increasing its acceleration ... 4 g at T+2 minutes 15 seconds. To reduce the g forces, the center engine was cut'.

checks.claim: Context: a steady push (the only force, in space) never gives a steady speed
David Scott, commander of Apollo 15, on the Moon in 1971, dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together
checks.note: NASA: Commander David Scott, end of the last moonwalk (EVA-3, 2 August 1971), 1.32-kg aluminium geological hammer and a falcon feather, live for the TV cameras. Grokipedia (Apollo 15) confirms Scott was commander and the 1971 mission; its EVA-1 and 1.8-kg details conflict with NASA but are not used in the question.

checks.claim: Stem: the Moon pulled on the hammer many times as hard, in proportion to its many times greater mass
checks.note: w = mg: pull in step with mass.

checks.claim: Key: same acceleration as the feather's
checks.note: Allen's report: 'the objects were observed to undergo the same acceleration and strike the lunar surface simultaneously'.

checks.claim: Wrong: many times / a little more / far less
checks.note: OpenStax: 'in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration g'. No air on the Moon, so 'a little more' is not defensible.

checks.claim: Context: televised; 'as Galileo had concluded long before'
checks.note: NASA: 'as Galileo had concluded hundreds of years before'. No Pisa legend is told.

checks.claim: Context: in a huge vacuum chamber in Ohio a bowling ball and feathers fall together under Earth's full gravity
checks.note: Brian Cox, BBC Human Universe (2014), NASA's Space Power Facility in Ohio, 'the world's biggest vacuum chamber'; they 'land at precisely the same time'.

checks.claim: Key: mass on the ISS is measured by a known push and the acceleration it gives
checks.note: NASA caption (11 Feb 2025): the device applies a known force and measures the resulting acceleration, a form of Newton's second law. Wikipedia (Human Research Facility 1): SLAMMD uses two springs on cams giving a constant force. (The Russian BMMD times a spring oscillation instead, but no choice describes that, so the key stands.)

checks.claim: Context: springs with a known push, motion tracked, a laptop works out mass to within about 0.2 kg
checks.note: Space.com: accuracy 'of half a pound (0.2 kilograms)'; Smithsonian also gives 0.5 lb. No NASA spec sheet found, but two outlets agree.

checks.claim: Wrong: pan balance / volume in a water tank / timing a drift to the floor
checks.note: In free fall nothing presses on a scale or pan and nothing drifts down; volume is not mass.

checks.claim: Context: 'In orbit his mass is unchanged but his weight all but vanishes'
checks.note: Under the definition this bank teaches (gravity-and-orbits, T3: 'weight, the pull of gravity') and OpenStax uses (w = mg), his weight does not vanish: NASA says gravity at the station is 'about 90 percent' of surface gravity and a 100-pound person 'would weigh 90 pounds' up there. What vanishes is the scale reading, because he and the station fall together; the bank's own T3 unit teaches exactly this against 'no gravity in space'. Fix: 'In orbit his mass is unchanged and Earth still pulls on him almost as hard as on the ground, but he and the station fall around Earth together, so he presses on nothing: neither pan of a balance would press down, and nothing drifts to the floor.'

checks.claim: Context: the space a body fills is its volume, not its mass
Key: the ball is fastest the instant it leaves the boot
checks.note: Kick biomechanics: the ball is accelerated only during the brief contact (9-12 ms), its speed still rising as the foot loses contact; after that only rolling resistance and air act against its motion on flat grass. (A ball given strong topspin can speed up after contact, as a billiard follow shot does, but that is an exotic case the stem does not set up.)

checks.claim: Wrong: midway through the push (the push still points forward, so it is still gaining speed)
checks.note: Acceleration points along the net force.

checks.claim: Wrong: a moment after it leaves / halfway along its roll
checks.note: No forward force acts once contact ends.

checks.claim: Context: medieval thinkers called the imagined carried force 'impetus', and many people still picture one
checks.note: Grokipedia: impetus is 'an impressed motive force' sustaining motion until resistance depletes it; Buridan (14th century) and Franciscus de Marchia gave it its medieval form (Philoponus earlier). Naive impetus beliefs in modern people: McCloskey's work, reviewed at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10607174 .

checks.claim: Key: net force and acceleration on the slowing ball both point back toward the pitcher
checks.note: Acceleration is 'in the same direction as the net external force'; the mitt's backward push dwarfs gravity.

checks.claim: Wrong: both forward / force back, acceleration forward / force forward, acceleration back
checks.note: Force and acceleration can never point opposite ways.

checks.claim: Context: the ball pushes forward on the mitt equally hard, but that force acts on the mitt
checks.note: Grokipedia: third-law pair forces 'act on different bodies and thus do not cancel'.

checks.claim: Key: equal and opposite forces; half the mass gets twice the acceleration
checks.note: Third law gives equal forces; second law gives a inversely proportional to m. The stem's premise (mutual push far larger than the ground's) makes the mutual push the net force.

checks.claim: Wrong: the same / half / four times
Context: many people expect the heavier one to push harder
checks.note: The 'dominance principle' misconception on the Force Concept Inventory's truck-and-car item.

checks.claim: Stem: plague shut Cambridge in 1665; Newton went home to the family farm at Woolsthorpe and worked on motion and gravity
checks.note: MacTutor: 'when the plague closed the University in the summer of 1665 ... he had to return to Lincolnshire'; Grokipedia (Woolsthorpe Manor): his birthplace, a yeoman farm with crops and livestock, where he stayed until spring 1667 and began on universal gravitation. Minor: Grokipedia (Isaac Newton) notes his Waste Book notes on circular motion date from 1664, so 'began' is a plain-words simplification for motion; acceptable.

checks.claim: Stem: in 1684 Halley asked what path a planet would follow under an inverse-square pull; Hooke and Wren had failed to settle it
checks.note: De Moivre's memorandum: Halley asked 'what he thought the curve would be that would be described by the Planets supposing the force of attraction towards the Sun to be reciprocal to the square of their distance'. Wikipedia (Principia): in January 1684 Hooke claimed the derivation, Wren was unconvinced, and Hooke never produced it. August 1684 per most authorities.

checks.claim: Key: Newton said he had worked it out but could not find the paper
checks.note: De Moivre: 'why saith he I have calculated it ... Sir Isaac looked among his papers but could not find it, but he promised him to renew it'. Wikipedia (Principia, Halley) agrees.

checks.claim: Wrong: read it in Kepler / guessed but not proved / tracked planets with his telescope
checks.note: Newton said 'I have calculated it'; Kepler fitted ellipses to Tycho's data without deriving them from an inverse-square force.

checks.claim: Context: November 1684 short paper on bodies in orbit; Halley persuaded him to write the full work
checks.note: 'sent to Edmond Halley in November 1684'; MacTutor: Halley 'persuaded Newton to write a full treatment'.

checks.claim: Context: 'the Principia of 1687, which opens with the three laws of motion'
checks.note: Grokipedia: the work 'opens with eight definitions'; the laws (as axioms) follow after a scholium on space and time. Wikipedia: it begins with 'Definitions' and 'Axioms or Laws of Motion'. Minor, but a historian would correct it. Fix: 'which sets out the three laws of motion near its start'.

checks.claim: Context: Kepler found the paths from observations without knowing the force; Hooke claimed the answer but never produced a proof
checks.note: Kepler did guess at a force from the Sun, but not its true law ('lacked a full mechanical framework'), so 'without knowing the force' holds. Hooke: Wikipedia (Principia).

checks.claim: Stem: the Royal Society agreed in 1686 to publish; Halley, who worked for the Society, paid the printing costs himself
checks.note: Ordered printed 19 May 1686; on 2 June 1686 the minutes record Halley would print it 'at his own charge'. Royal Society: Halley was 'then Clerk at the Royal Society' and paid 'much of the money ... from his own pocket'.

checks.claim: Key: the Society had spent its money on a book about fish (Willughby's De Historia Piscium)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the Society withdrew its funding after spending on Willughby's De historia piscium (1686). Wikipedia: 'had just spent its book budget on De Historia piscium'. Royal Society 2012: it 'nearly bankrupted the Society'.

checks.claim: Wrong: a great telescope / the Great Fire of London / taking Hooke's side
checks.note: No source gives any of these as the reason.

checks.claim: Context: History of Fishes lavishly illustrated and sold badly
checks.note: Royal Society: 'lavishly illustrated', 'did not prove to be the publishing sensation that the Fellows had hoped'. Willughby began it; John Ray finished it after his death; crediting Willughby is standard.

checks.claim: Context: 'Halley was later given 75 unsold copies of it'
checks.note: The Council minutes (Birch, 6 July 1687, quoted there) give 'fifty copies of the History of Fishes ... instead of the fifty pounds ordered him' plus 'a gratuity of twenty other copies': 70, not 75 (also https://note.com/reading_monkey/n/nb12438b45072). The 75 is only in an unsourced Wikipedia (Halley) footnote. Fix: drop the number: 'and Halley was later paid in unsold copies of it in place of his salary'.

checks.claim: Context: Halley read the proofs; Newton threatened to leave out Book 3 over Hooke's claim; Halley talked him round; the whole Principia appeared in 1687
checks.note: Wikipedia: Newton 'threatened to withdraw and suppress Book 3 altogether'; Halley persuaded him; complete work appeared July 1687. Grokipedia: Halley 'proofread the galleys'.

unit_notes: Physics of all seven scenes holds. Three context errors, no key or choice errors: (1) e422397088 says the astronaut's weight 'all but vanishes' in orbit, which contradicts the bank's own definition of weight as gravity's pull (gravity-and-orbits, T3) and NASA's '90 percent'; reword to free fall. (2) acbc7ab76d says the Principia 'opens with' the three laws; it opens with eight definitions. (3) 7272b2b2bd's '75 unsold copies': the Society's minutes give 50 plus 20; drop the number. The facts sheet's F21 carries the 75 from Wikipedia and F12 the 'effectively weightless' framing; both should follow the fixes.
